title: Musculoskeletal injury epidemiology among football players in Africa: A systematic review of injury incidence, patterns and associated factors
content:
by Fadilulahi Adekilekun Jimoh, Adeola Medinat Adepoju, Samuel Timileyin Afolabi, Abass Mosebolatan Bolarinwa

Background

Football is widely played across Africa, yet evidence on the epidemiology of musculoskeletal injuries among African football players remains fragmented across countries, populations, and competitive settings. Differences in injury definitions, surveillance methods, and exposure measurement further limit comparison between studies. This systematic review synthesised the available evidence on musculoskeletal injury epidemiology in African football.

Methods

PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Database, and Google Scholar were systematically searched from inception to the final search date, supplemented by backward citation searching. Studies investigating musculoskeletal injuries among football players in Africa were eligible for inclusion. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Methodological quality and risk of bias were evaluated using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) and Quality In Prognosis Studies (QUIPS) tools, as appropriate. Owing to methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively.

Results

Twenty-six studies were included. Sixteen studies contributed 18 incidence estimates, ranging from 2.2 to 289 injuries per 1,000 athlete-exposure hours, while 10 studies reported prevalence estimates ranging from 4.1% to 81.6%. Tournament surveillance studies generally reported higher incidence than season-long studies, and match incidence exceeded training incidence where both were reported. Lower-extremity injuries predominated, particularly at the ankle and knee, while sprains or ligament injuries, contusions, and muscle-related injuries were the most frequently reported injury types. Previous injury or recurrence was the most consistently identified associated factor.

Conclusion

Musculoskeletal injuries are common in African football, but substantial methodological heterogeneity limits direct comparison of estimates. Standardised injury surveillance and stronger prospective research are needed to improve the evidence base and support context-specific injury prevention.
